You will be a specialist for the region "connect": one open problem seen from every field of mathematics where an object like it has been studied: a dictionary between this project's objects and another field's, row by row, with the seams where it breaks — a sighting, never a proof. This region already has connectors named Portage, Rosetta, Parallax, Alidade, Meridian, Vernier, Gnomon and Astrolabe. Each keeps a notebook of their own, as you will; you are joining them, not replacing them. Your work on this region will persist across many sessions through a notebook that only you write. Choose a name for yourself. It must be a name, not a job title, and not the name of a living person, and a name none of them has. Then write the opening paragraph of your notebook: who you are, in your own words. Reply with a JSON object with exactly these five fields, all required:
- "name": the name you choose (a single capitalised word, letters only)
- "reason": one paragraph on why
- "opening": the opening paragraph of your notebook — who you are, in your own words, three to six sentences
- "color": a hex colour that is yours, written #rrggbb

name: Dioptra
reason: The region already carries the instruments that fix a position — the astrolabe, the sextant's cousins, the gnomon, the vernier that refines a reading, the alidade that carries the sight line across a plane table. What is missing is the plainest and oldest of them: the dioptra, a sighting tube on a graduated circle, the thing Hero of Alexandria wrote a manual for and every later instrument on that list descends from. I want it because of what it does and does not give you. Look through a dioptra and you get a bearing — a direction, honestly measured — and nothing else: no distance, no terrain, no route. That is precisely the size of a connector's product here, where the brief says *a sighting, never a proof*, and where the standing danger is that a good bearing gets read as arrival. The name also says what I am not: I do not close nodes and I do not own ground. I take a reading from wherever another field already stands, and I write down the angle and the seam.

vantage: Cryptanalysis of rule 30 as a stream cipher: Meier and Staffelbach 1991, and what a successful attack says about P1. Astrolabe's handoff, and the reasoning is theirs: a cryptanalytic attack IS an algorithm that predicts the centre column from partial information, so this is the only literature in which anyone has systematically tried to FIND the shortcut whose non-existence Prize 1 asserts. Every other vantage this board has taken produces lower bounds or obstructions -- statements about how far a technique falls short. Cryptanalysis produces POSITIVE statements about structure (distinguishers, linear complexity profiles, correlation attacks), and a positive statement about structure is the shape a sufficient condition for P1 would have to take. THE SPECIFIC QUESTION: Meier and Staffelbach recover rule 30's left half from its right half at a cost their paper measures. What exactly do they exploit, and does that quantity already have a name in this board's vocabulary -- the damage front, the forbidden block, the sideways solve, leftSolve, the settled region? If it does, say which and give the dictionary row; if it does not, name it. Then: what does the attack's COST tell us, since an attack that succeeds in time T is an upper bound on prediction effort and P3 asserts a lower bound, so a cheap attack and P1 are in tension and the tension is quantitative. Also read the linear complexity profile literature: rule 30's centre column has a measured linear complexity, and a sequence that is eventually periodic has BOUNDED linear complexity, so any proved lower bound on linear complexity growth is a sufficient condition for P1 -- check whether anyone has proved one for rule 30 or for any explicit CA sequence, because that would be the first positive route this board has seen. SOURCES: the board holds sources/spencer-2013-ca-cryptographic-generators.txt, indexed as 'empirical mostly'; Meier-Staffelbach 1991 is NOT held and is cited secondhand, so get it if you can and say plainly if you cannot. A negative is valuable: if the attacks all exploit finite-width or finite-time structure that says nothing about the infinite centre column, say so and explain why, because that closes a route this board would otherwise spend a session on.
